# function to create labeled barplots


def labeled_barplot(data, feature, perc=False, n=None):
    """
    Barplot with percentage at the top

    data: dataframe
    feature: dataframe column
    perc: whether to display percentages instead of count (default is False)
    n: displays the top n category levels (default is None, i.e., display all levels)
    """

    total = len(data[feature])  # length of the column
    count = data[feature].nunique()
    if n is None:
        plt.figure(figsize=(count + 1, 5))
    else:
        plt.figure(figsize=(n + 1, 5))

    plt.xticks(rotation=90, fontsize=15)
    ax = sns.countplot(
        data=data,
        x=feature,
        palette="Paired",
        order=data[feature].value_counts().index[:n].sort_values(),
    )

    for p in ax.patches:
        if perc == True:
            label = "{:.1f}%".format(
                100 * p.get_height() / total
            )  # percentage of each class of the category
        else:
            label = p.get_height()  # count of each level of the category

        x = p.get_x() + p.get_width() / 2  # width of the plot
        y = p.get_height()  # height of the plot

        ax.annotate(
            label,
            (x, y),
            ha="center",
            va="center",
            size=12,
            xytext=(0, 5),
            textcoords="offset points",
        )  # annotate the percentage

    plt.show()  # show the plot
In [94]:
def histogram_boxplot(data, feature, figsize=(15, 10), kde=False, bins=None):
    """
    Boxplot and histogram combined

    data: dataframe
    feature: dataframe column
    figsize: size of figure (default (15,10))
    kde: whether to show the density curve (default False)
    bins: number of bins for histogram (default None)
    """
    f2, (ax_box2, ax_hist2) = plt.subplots(
        nrows=2,  # Number of rows of the subplot grid= 2
        sharex=True,  # x-axis will be shared among all subplots
        gridspec_kw={"height_ratios": (0.25, 0.75)},
        figsize=figsize,
    )  # creating the 2 subplots
    sns.boxplot(
        data=data, x=feature, ax=ax_box2, showmeans=True, color="violet"
    )  # boxplot will be created and a triangle will indicate the mean value of the column
    sns.histplot(
        data=data, x=feature, kde=kde, ax=ax_hist2, bins=bins
    ) if bins else sns.histplot(
        data=data, x=feature, kde=kde, ax=ax_hist2
    )  # For histogram
    ax_hist2.axvline(
        data[feature].mean(), color="green", linestyle="--"
    )  # Add mean to the histogram
    ax_hist2.axvline(
        data[feature].median(), color="black", linestyle="-"
    )  # Add median to the histogram

Based on the combined histogram and boxplot for no_of_employees, the following observations can be made:¶

Extreme Right Skewness: The histogram is heavily right-skewed, with a large number of companies having a relatively small number of employees. The frequency drops sharply as the employee count increases, indicating that very large companies are rare in this dataset.¶
Presence of Outliers: The boxplot clearly reveals numerous outliers on the upper end of the distribution. These outliers represent a small number of companies with significantly larger employee counts compared to the majority, confirming the presence of a few exceptionally large organizations in the dataset.¶
Mean vs. Median: The mean (green dashed line) is considerably greater than the median (black solid line), which is a strong indicator of the right-skewed distribution and reflects the disproportionate influence of high-value outliers on the mean.¶
This distribution implies that while the majority of visa applications are associated with smaller companies, a small number of very large organizations are also represented. The pronounced skewness suggests that preprocessing steps such as log transformation or the use of robust statistical methods may be necessary during model training to prevent the model from being unduly influenced by these large employer outliers.¶

Overall, the data reflects a dynamic organizational landscape dominated by modern companies, while still including a notable number of long-standing establishments. Appropriate strategies such as oversampling (e.g., SMOTE), undersampling, or class weighting will need to be considered and applied during model training to ensure fair and reliable predictions across both classes.¶

### function to plot distributions wrt target


def distribution_plot_wrt_target(data, predictor, target):

    fig, axs = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(12, 10))

    target_uniq = data[target].unique()

    axs[0, 0].set_title("Distribution of target for target=" + str(target_uniq[0]))
    sns.histplot(
        data=data[data[target] == target_uniq[0]],
        x=predictor,
        kde=True,
        ax=axs[0, 0],
        color="teal",
        stat="density",
    )

    axs[0, 1].set_title("Distribution of target for target=" + str(target_uniq[1]))
    sns.histplot(
        data=data[data[target] == target_uniq[1]],
        x=predictor,
        kde=True,
        ax=axs[0, 1],
        color="orange",
        stat="density",
    )

    axs[1, 0].set_title("Boxplot w.r.t target")
    sns.boxplot(data=data, x=target, y=predictor, ax=axs[1, 0], palette="gist_rainbow")

    axs[1, 1].set_title("Boxplot (without outliers) w.r.t target")
    sns.boxplot(
        data=data,
        x=target,
        y=predictor,
        ax=axs[1, 1],
        showfliers=False,
        palette="gist_rainbow",
    )

    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()

def stacked_barplot(data, predictor, target):
    """
    Print the category counts and plot a stacked bar chart

    data: dataframe
    predictor: independent variable
    target: target variable
    """
    count = data[predictor].nunique()
    sorter = data[target].value_counts().index[-1]
    tab1 = pd.crosstab(data[predictor], data[target], margins=True).sort_values(
        by=sorter, ascending=False
    )
    print(tab1)
    print("-" * 120)
    tab = pd.crosstab(data[predictor], data[target], normalize="index").sort_values(
        by=sorter, ascending=False
    )
    tab.plot(kind="bar", stacked=True, figsize=(count + 5, 5))
    plt.legend(
        loc="lower left", frameon=False,
    )
    plt.legend(loc="upper left", bbox_to_anchor=(1, 1))
    plt.show()

Let's find out if education has any impact on visa certification¶

In [105]:

case_status            Certified  Denied    All

Master's                    7575    2059   9634

Based on the stacked bar plot of education_of_employee against case_status, the following observations can be made:¶

Higher Education, Higher Certification Rate: Applicants holding Master's and Doctorate degrees demonstrate significantly higher certification rates compared to those with Bachelor's or High School education. Doctorate holders record the highest success rate at over 85% (1,912 Certified vs. 280 Denied), while Master's degree holders also perform strongly (7,575 Certified vs. 2,059 Denied). This likely reflects the specialized nature of the roles associated with advanced degrees, making it considerably easier for the Department of Labor to justify that no suitably qualified local worker is available to fill the position.¶
Bachelor's Degree: Although Bachelor's degree holders represent the largest group of applicants, their certification rate of approximately 62% falls slightly below the overall dataset average of 66.8%, with a notably higher proportion of denials compared to Master's and Doctorate holders (6,367 Certified vs. 3,867 Denied). This suggests that a Bachelor's degree may serve as the minimum educational threshold for many visa applications, but is not in itself a strong guarantee of certification success.¶
High School Education: Applicants with only a High School education have the lowest certification rate and the highest denial rate proportionally, with just 34% of applications being certified (1,164 Certified vs. 2,256 Denied). This indicates that a high school education alone is generally insufficient for visa certification in this dataset, reflecting a strong preference for higher academic qualifications. The roles typically associated with this education level are often considered non-specialized, making certification considerably more difficult to obtain and rendering a high school qualification a significant risk factor for denial.¶
Inference: There is a clear positive relationship between education level and the likelihood of visa certification. Higher educational qualifications — particularly Master's and Doctorate degrees — represent a significant advantage in the visa application process, while lower qualifications, especially at the High School level, are strongly associated with higher denial rates.¶

Inference: While regional differences in median prevailing wages do exist, the wide wage ranges, consistent right skewness, and prevalence of high-end outliers across all regions suggest that job-specific factors — such as skill level, industry, and degree of specialization — are at least as influential as, if not more so than, geographic region in determining prevailing wage. This implies that prevailing_wage may carry stronger predictive signal when considered alongside role-specific features rather than in isolation.¶

Data Preparation for modeling¶

We want to predict which visa will be certified.¶

Before we proceed to build a model, we'll have to encode categorical features.¶

We'll split the data into train and test to be able to evaluate the model that we build on the train data.¶

In [115]:
data["case_status"] = data["case_status"].apply(lambda x: 1 if x == "Certified" else 0)

X = data.drop(["case_status"], axis=1)
y = data["case_status"]

# X = X.astype(float)

    X, y, test_size=0.2, random_state=1, stratify=y
)

# then we split the temporary set into train and validation

X_train, X_val, y_train, y_val = train_test_split(
    X_temp, y_temp, test_size=0.25, random_state=1, stratify=y_temp
)

Model Building¶

Model evaluation criterion¶

Model can make wrong predictions as:

The model predicts that the visa application will get certified, but in reality, the visa application gets denied.

Model predicts that the visa application will not get certified but in reality, the visa application get certified. Which case is more important?

Both cases are important as:

If a visa is certified when it should be denied, the wrong employee will get the job position, while US citizens will miss the opportunity to work in that position.

If a visa is denied when it had to be certified, the U.S. will lose a suitable human resource that can contribute to the economy.

How to reduce the losses?

F1 Score can be used as a metric for evaluation of the model; the greater the F1 score, the higher the chances of minimizing False Negatives and False Positives.

We will use balanced class weights so that the model focuses equally on both classes.

First, let's create functions to calculate different metrics and a confusion matrix so that we don't have to use the same code repeatedly for each model.

The model_performance_classification_sklearn function will be used to check the model performance of models.

The confusion_matrix_sklearn function will be used to plot the confusion matrix.

In [117]:
# defining a function to compute different metrics to check performance of a classification model built using sklearn


def model_performance_classification_sklearn(model, predictors, target):
    """
    Function to compute different metrics to check classification model performance

    model: classifier
    predictors: independent variables
    target: dependent variable
    """

    # predicting using the independent variables
    pred = model.predict(predictors)

    acc = accuracy_score(target, pred)  # to compute Accuracy
    recall = recall_score(target, pred)  # to compute Recall
    precision = precision_score(target, pred)  # to compute Precision
    f1 = f1_score(target, pred)  # to compute F1-score

    # creating a dataframe of metrics
    df_perf = pd.DataFrame(
        {"Accuracy": acc, "Recall": recall, "Precision": precision, "F1": f1,},
        index=[0],
    )

    return df_perf

Model Building - Original Data¶

In [118]:
# The Models (Different algorithms)
from sklearn.ensemble import BaggingClassifier, RandomForestClassifier, GradientBoostingClassifier, AdaBoostClassifier
from xgboost import XGBClassifier

# The Grading Scale (To see if they are right)
from sklearn.metrics import f1_score, accuracy_score, recall_score, precision_score, confusion_matrix

# Tools for plotting
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns
In [119]:
models = []

# 1. Bagging: Takes a vote among many trees
models.append(("Bagging", BaggingClassifier(random_state=1)))

# 2. Random Forest: A smarter version of Bagging
models.append(("Random Forest", RandomForestClassifier(random_state=1, class_weight="balanced")))

# 3. GBM: Builds trees one after another to fix errors
models.append(("GBM", GradientBoostingClassifier(random_state=1)))

# 4. AdaBoost: Focuses heavily on the 'hard' cases
models.append(("Adaboost", AdaBoostClassifier(random_state=1)))

# 5. XGBoost: The fastest and usually the most accurate booster
models.append(("XGBoost", XGBClassifier(random_state=1, eval_metric='logloss')))

print("\n" "Training Performance:" "\n")
for name, model in models:
    model.fit(X_train, y_train)
    scores = f1_score(y_train, model.predict(X_train))
    print("{}: {}".format(name, scores))

print("\n" "Validation Performance:" "\n")

for name, model in models:
    model.fit(X_train, y_train)
    scores_val = f1_score(y_val, model.predict(X_val))
    print("{}: {}".format(name, scores_val))

print(f"{'Model Name':<15} | {'Train F1':<10} | {'Val F1':<10} | {'Difference':<10}")
print("-" * 55)

for name, model in models:
    # 1. Fit the model
    model.fit(X_train, y_train)
    
    # 2. Get predictions for both sets
    train_pred = model.predict(X_train)
    val_pred = model.predict(X_val)
    
    # 3. Calculate F1-scores
    f1_train = f1_score(y_train, train_pred)
    f1_val = f1_score(y_val, val_pred)
    
    # 4. Calculate the difference (the "Overfitting Gap")
    diff = f1_train - f1_val
    
    print(f"{name:<15} | {f1_train:<10.4f} | {f1_val:<10.4f} | {diff:<10.4f}")

-------------------------------------------------------
Bagging         | 0.9891     | 0.7738     | 0.2153

GBM             | 0.8291     | 0.8266     | 0.0025

Based on the F1 scores from the training and validation sets, the following observations can be made regarding model performance:¶

Significant Overfitting in Bagging and Random Forest: Both the Bagging and Random Forest models achieve very high F1 scores on the training data (Bagging: 0.9891, Random Forest: 1.0000), but their performance drops considerably on the validation set (Bagging: 0.7737, Random Forest: 0.8048). The large gap between training and validation scores (Bagging: 0.2153, Random Forest: 0.1952) is a strong indicator of overfitting — both models have memorized the training data rather than learning generalizable patterns, resulting in poor performance on unseen data.¶
Strong Generalization in GBM and AdaBoost: The Gradient Boosting Machine (GBM) and AdaBoost models demonstrate highly consistent F1 scores across both the training and validation sets, with minimal differences of 0.0025 and 0.0024, respectively. This negligible gap between training and validation performance suggests that both models are generalizing effectively to unseen data with little to no overfitting.¶
Moderate Overfitting in XGBoost: XGBoost achieves a solid training F1 score of 0.8963, but records a noticeable drop to 0.8079 on the validation set — a difference of 0.0884. While this indicates some degree of overfitting, it is considerably less severe than that observed in the Bagging and Random Forest models, positioning XGBoost as a middle ground between the extremes.¶
Best Validation Performance — GBM: Among all models evaluated, the Gradient Boosting Machine achieves the highest validation F1 score of 0.8266, closely followed by AdaBoost at 0.8180. This suggests that GBM currently offers the best balance between bias and variance for this dataset, making it the most robust and reliable model at this stage of evaluation.¶

Model Building - Oversampled Data¶

# 1. Complete the model list
models = []
models.append(("Bagging", BaggingClassifier(random_state=1)))
models.append(("Random Forest", RandomForestClassifier(random_state=1)))
models.append(("GBM", GradientBoostingClassifier(random_state=1)))
models.append(("Adaboost", AdaBoostClassifier(random_state=1)))
models.append(("XGBoost", XGBClassifier(random_state=1, eval_metric='logloss')))

print("\n" "Training Performance (Oversampled Data):" "\n")
for name, model in models:
    # We train on the NEW oversampled data
    model.fit(X_train_over, y_train_over)
    
    # We check the score on the SAME oversampled data
    scores = f1_score(y_train_over, model.predict(X_train_over))
    print("{}: {:.4f}".format(name, scores))

print("\n" "Validation Performance (Original Data):" "\n")
for name, model in models:
    # Note: The model is already trained from the loop above, 
    # but we test it on the UNTOUCHED validation set.
    scores = f1_score(y_val, model.predict(X_val))
    print("{}: {:.4f}".format(name, scores))

for name, model in models:
    # 1. Train on the synthetic oversampled data
    model.fit(X_train_over, y_train_over)
    
    # 2. Get predictions
    train_pred = model.predict(X_train_over)
    val_pred = model.predict(X_val)
    
    # 3. Calculate F1-scores
    f1_train = f1_score(y_train_over, train_pred)
    f1_val = f1_score(y_val, val_pred)
    
    # 4. Calculate the difference
    diff = f1_train - f1_val
    
    print(f"{name:<15} | {f1_train:<15.4f} | {f1_val:<15.4f} | {diff:<10.4f}")

-----------------------------------------------------------------
Bagging         | 0.9877          | 0.7682          | 0.2195    
Random Forest   | 1.0000          | 0.7953          | 0.2047    
GBM             | 0.8072          | 0.8173          | -0.0101   
Adaboost        | 0.8005          | 0.8195          | -0.0190   
XGBoost         | 0.8709          | 0.8129          | 0.0579

Based on the F1 scores following oversampling with SMOTE, the following observations can be made:¶

Best Overall Performance — AdaBoost: AdaBoost emerges as the best-performing model after oversampling, achieving the highest validation F1 score of 0.8195. Notably, its training F1 (0.8005) and validation F1 (0.8195) are remarkably close, yielding a negative difference of -0.0190. This near-identical performance across both sets is a strong indicator of excellent generalization, confirming that AdaBoost is not overfitting the training data.¶
Strong Performance from GBM and XGBoost: The Gradient Boosting Machine (GBM) continues to perform strongly, recording a validation F1 of 0.8173 and an even smaller training-to-validation difference of -0.0101, reflecting outstanding generalization. XGBoost also delivers a competitive validation F1 of 0.8129, though its slightly larger difference of 0.0579 suggests a minor degree of overfitting relative to AdaBoost and GBM — an issue that may be addressable through further hyperparameter tuning.¶
Persistent Overfitting in Bagging and Random Forest: Despite the introduction of SMOTE, the Bagging and Random Forest models continue to exhibit significant overfitting, with notably high training F1 scores that fail to translate into comparable validation performance. The large gap between their training and validation scores remains a concern, and these models lag behind the ensemble boosting methods in terms of generalization ability.¶
Impact of SMOTE on Model Performance: Prior to oversampling, GBM held a marginal lead in validation performance. However, the introduction of additional Denied examples via SMOTE appears to have particularly benefited AdaBoost, which is architecturally designed to focus on difficult-to-classify instances. By exposing AdaBoost to a more balanced representation of the minority class, SMOTE enabled the model to refine its decision boundaries for Denied cases more effectively, ultimately allowing it to surpass GBM as the top-performing model.¶
Overall: The application of SMOTE has produced a meaningful shift in the model rankings, with AdaBoost emerging as the strongest performer in terms of both validation F1 score and generalization. GBM remains a close and reliable alternative, while XGBoost warrants further tuning. Bagging and Random Forest continue to underperform relative to the boosting-based models and may require more aggressive regularization or alternative resampling strategies to address their persistent overfitting.¶

Based on the undersampling results, the following observations can be made by comparing validation F1 scores across all three data preparation methods:¶

ModelOriginal Data (Val F1) SMOTE Oversampled (Val F1) Undersampled (Val F1)¶
GBM 0.8266, 0.8173, 0.7766¶
AdaBoost 0.8180, 0.8195, 0.7660¶
Overall Decrease in Validation F1 Scores: Compared to both the original and oversampled data, the validation F1 scores for most models decline notably when trained on undersampled data. This suggests that removing thousands of Certified examples in order to balance the classes deprives the models of valuable information needed to understand the nuances of the certification decision, ultimately resulting in poorer performance on the validation set.¶
Underfitting in GBM and AdaBoost: The training F1 scores for GBM (0.7281) and AdaBoost (0.7015) are considerably lower than those achieved under SMOTE or the original data. These reduced training scores indicate that both models are underfitting — a direct consequence of having insufficient training examples to learn the underlying patterns of the data effectively.¶
Persistent Overfitting in Random Forest: Despite the significant reduction in training data size introduced by undersampling, Random Forest continues to achieve a perfect training F1 score of 1.0000. This confirms that the model is still memorizing the training rows rather than learning generalizable decision logic — a persistent weakness that undersampling alone is insufficient to resolve.¶
Good Generalization but Lower Scores in GBM and AdaBoost: GBM and AdaBoost continue to demonstrate strong generalization under undersampling, with negative training-to-validation differences of -0.0485 and -0.0645, respectively, confirming the absence of overfitting. However, their validation F1 scores (GBM: 0.7766, AdaBoost: 0.7660) fall meaningfully short of what both models achieved with the original and oversampled data, indicating that good generalization alone is not sufficient when the underlying training signal is too weak.¶
Final Decision: Based on the comparative results across all three approaches, the original data and SMOTE oversampling are the clear preferred strategies, both delivering higher and more stable validation F1 scores than undersampling.¶
Between the two: The original data yielded a slightly higher validation F1 for GBM (0.8266).¶
SMOTE produced a marginally better result for AdaBoost (0.8195) and is likely to improve the model's ability to correctly identify Denied cases by providing a more balanced representation of the minority class during training.¶
Inference: Undersampling has generally proven detrimental in this context, leading to a consistent decline in validation F1 scores across all models relative to the original and oversampled data. While undersampling is a valid technique for addressing class imbalance, the reduction in overall training data size in this case appears to have hindered the models' ability to learn complex relationships within the data. Oversampling via SMOTE offers a more effective balance between class representation and data richness, and alongside the original data, represents the stronger foundation for final model selection and hyperparameter tuning.¶

from sklearn import metrics
from sklearn.model_selection import GridSearchCV
import numpy as np

%%time
# Choose the type of classifier.
rf_tuned = RandomForestClassifier(random_state=1, oob_score=True, bootstrap=True)

parameters = {
    "max_depth": list(np.arange(5, 15, 5)),
    "max_features": ["sqrt", "log2"],
    "min_samples_split": [3, 5, 7],
    "n_estimators": np.arange(10, 40, 10),
}

# Type of scoring used to compare parameter combinations
acc_scorer = metrics.make_scorer(metrics.f1_score)

# Run the grid search
grid_obj = GridSearchCV(rf_tuned, parameters, scoring=acc_scorer, cv=5, n_jobs=-1)
grid_obj = grid_obj.fit(X_train_over, y_train_over)

# Set the clf to the best combination of parameters
rf_tuned = grid_obj.best_estimator_

# Fit the best algorithm to the data.
rf_tuned.fit(X_train, y_train)

min_impurity_decrease min_impurity_decrease: float, default=0.0

A node will be split if this split induces a decrease of the impurity
greater than or equal to this value.

The weighted impurity decrease equation is the following::

N_t / N * (impurity - N_t_R / N_t * right_impurity
- N_t_L / N_t * left_impurity)

samples at the current node, ``N_t_L`` is the number of samples in the
left child, and ``N_t_R`` is the number of samples in the right child.

if ``sample_weight`` is passed.

class_weight class_weight: {"balanced", "balanced_subsample"}, dict or list of dicts, default=None

Weights associated with classes in the form ``{class_label: weight}``.
If not given, all classes are supposed to have weight one. For
multi-output problems, a list of dicts can be provided in the same
order as the columns of y.

Note that for multioutput (including multilabel) weights should be
defined for each class of every column in its own dict. For example,
for four-class multilabel classification weights should be
[{0: 1, 1: 1}, {0: 1, 1: 5}, {0: 1, 1: 1}, {0: 1, 1: 1}] instead of
[{1:1}, {2:5}, {3:1}, {4:1}].

The "balanced" mode uses the values of y to automatically adjust
weights inversely proportional to class frequencies in the input data
as ``n_samples / (n_classes * np.bincount(y))``

The "balanced_subsample" mode is the same as "balanced" except that
weights are computed based on the bootstrap sample for every tree

Indicates the monotonicity constraint to enforce on each feature.

If monotonic_cst is None, no constraints are applied.

Monotonicity constraints are not supported for:

Checking model performance on training set¶

In [156]:
from sklearn.metrics import confusion_matrix
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns
import numpy as np

# 1. Get predictions
y_pred = rf_tuned.predict(X_train)

# 2. Create the raw confusion matrix
cm = confusion_matrix(y_train, y_pred)

# 3. Calculate percentages
# We divide each box by the total sum of all boxes
cm_percent = cm.astype('float') / cm.sum() * 100

# 4. Create labels combining Count and Percentage
# This creates strings like "1500 \n (45.2%)"
labels = (np.array(["{0:d}\n({1:.2f}%)".format(count, percent) 
          for count, percent in zip(cm.flatten(), cm_percent.flatten())]
         )).reshape(2,2)

# 5. Plot using Seaborn for better control
plt.figure(figsize=(8, 6))
sns.heatmap(cm, annot=labels, fmt="", cmap='Blues', cbar=False,
            xticklabels=["Denied", "Certified"], 
            yticklabels=["Denied", "Certified"])

plt.xlabel('Predicted Label')
plt.ylabel('True Label')
plt.title('Confusion Matrix: Counts & Percentages')
plt.show()

Checking model performance on validation set¶

In [158]:
import seaborn as sns
import numpy as np
from sklearn.metrics import confusion_matrix
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# 1. Generate predictions for the Validation set
y_pred = rf_tuned.predict(X_val)

# 2. Compute the confusion matrix
cm = confusion_matrix(y_val, y_pred)

# 3. Calculate percentages (relative to the total number of cases)
# This gives you the 'Global' percentage for each box
cm_percent = cm.astype('float') / cm.sum() * 100

# 4. Create the labels: "Count \n (Percentage%)"
labels = (np.array(["{0:d}\n({1:.2f}%)".format(count, percent) 
          for count, percent in zip(cm.flatten(), cm_percent.flatten())]
         )).reshape(2,2)

# 5. Plot using a heatmap
plt.figure(figsize=(8, 5))
sns.heatmap(cm, annot=labels, fmt="", cmap='Blues', cbar=False,
            xticklabels=["Denied", "Certified"], 
            yticklabels=["Denied", "Certified"])

plt.title("Tuned Random Forest: Validation Performance")
plt.xlabel("Predicted Outcome")
plt.ylabel("Actual Outcome")
plt.show()

Based on the tuned Random Forest model's performance on both the training and validation sets, the following observations can be made:¶

F1 Score: The tuned Random Forest model achieves an F1 score of 0.8449 on the training set and 0.8262 on the validation set, representing a difference of only 0.0187. This negligible gap between training and validation performance indicates that hyperparameter tuning has been effective in significantly reducing the overfitting that was previously observed in the untuned model, resulting in considerably improved generalization to unseen data.¶
Recall: The model records a high recall score of 0.9112 on the training set and 0.8904 on the validation set. The consistency of these scores across both sets confirms that the model is effectively identifying a large proportion of actual Certified cases, with very few true positives being missed.¶
Precision: Precision scores of 0.7877 on the training set and 0.7707 on the validation set, while slightly lower than the corresponding recall scores, remain at a solid level. This indicates a relatively low rate of false positives — meaning the model is not excessively certifying applications that should have been denied.¶
Overall: Hyperparameter tuning has meaningfully improved the Random Forest model's generalization capability, substantially closing the training-to-validation performance gap that characterized the untuned version. With strong and consistent recall scores, solid precision, and a well-balanced F1 score on the validation set, the tuned Random Forest model emerges as a strong candidate for predicting visa certification outcomes — effectively balancing the trade-off between precision and recall.¶

Based on the tuned AdaBoost Classifier's performance on both the training and validation sets, the following observations can be made:¶

F1 Score: The tuned AdaBoost Classifier achieves an F1 score of 0.8235 on the training set and 0.8231 on the validation set, with a negligible difference of just 0.0004 between the two. This near-identical performance across both sets is a strong indicator of excellent generalization, confirming that the model is learning robust and transferable patterns rather than memorizing the training data. Virtually no overfitting is observed.¶
Recall: The model records consistently high recall scores of 0.8762 on the training set and 0.8725 on the validation set. The minimal drop between the two confirms that the model is highly effective at correctly identifying the majority of actual Certified visa applications, with very few true positives being missed across both sets.¶
Precision: Precision scores of 0.7767 on the training set and 0.7789 on the validation set are not only solid in absolute terms but also noteworthy in that the validation precision marginally exceeds the training precision. This slight improvement on unseen data suggests that the model's positive predictions are reliable and that the rate of false positives remains well controlled.¶
Inference: The tuned AdaBoost Classifier distinguishes itself through its exceptional generalization and well-balanced performance across all three metrics. The near-zero gap between training and validation F1 scores (0.0004) represents the smallest overfitting margin observed among all models evaluated, making it the most stable and consistent performer in this analysis. While its absolute F1 scores are comparable to those of the tuned Random Forest model, AdaBoost's significantly tighter training-to-validation gap gives it a meaningful edge in terms of reliability and robustness — qualities that are particularly valuable when deploying a model to predict outcomes on truly unseen data.¶

Maximum depth of the individual regression estimators. The maximum

for best performance; the best value depends on the interaction

A node will be split if this split induces a decrease of the impurity
greater than or equal to this value.
Values must be in the range `[0.0, inf)`.

The weighted impurity decrease equation is the following::

N_t / N * (impurity - N_t_R / N_t * right_impurity
- N_t_L / N_t * left_impurity)

where ``N`` is the total number of samples, ``N_t`` is the number of
samples at the current node, ``N_t_L`` is the number of samples in the
left child, and ``N_t_R`` is the number of samples in the right child.

if ``sample_weight`` is passed.

from sklearn.metrics import confusion_matrix
import seaborn as sns
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# 1. Generate predictions using your tuned GBC model
y_pred_train = gbc_tuned.predict(X_train)

# 2. Compute the confusion matrix
cm = confusion_matrix(y_train, y_pred_train)

# 3. Calculate percentages relative to the total samples
cm_percent = cm.astype('float') / cm.sum() * 100

# 4. Create text labels: "Count \n (Percentage%)"
labels = (np.array(["{0:d}\n({1:.2f}%)".format(count, percent) 
          for count, percent in zip(cm.flatten(), cm_percent.flatten())]
         )).reshape(2,2)

# 5. Plotting
plt.figure(figsize=(7, 5))
sns.heatmap(cm, annot=labels, fmt="", cmap='Oranges', cbar=False,
            xticklabels=["Denied", "Certified"], 
            yticklabels=["Denied", "Certified"])

plt.title("Confusion Matrix: Tuned GBC (Training Set)")
plt.xlabel("Predicted Outcome")
plt.ylabel("Actual Outcome")
plt.show()

Based on the tuned Gradient Boosting Classifier's performance on both the training and validation sets, the following observations can be made:¶

F1 Score: The tuned Gradient Boosting Classifier achieves an F1 score of 0.8276 on the training set and 0.8269 on the validation set, with a negligible difference of just 0.0007 between the two. This near-identical performance across both sets is a strong indicator of excellent generalization, confirming that the model has learned robust and transferable patterns with virtually no overfitting.¶
Recall: The model records consistently high recall scores of 0.8991 on the training set and 0.8975 on the validation set — the highest recall figures observed among all tuned models evaluated. The minimal drop between the two sets confirms that the model is highly effective at correctly identifying the vast majority of actual Certified visa applications, with very few true positives being missed.¶
Precision: The model achieves identical precision scores of 0.7666 on both the training and validation sets — a particularly noteworthy result, as it demonstrates perfect consistency in the model's positive prediction reliability across seen and unseen data. This indicates a well-controlled rate of false positives and confirms that the model's predictions are stable and dependable.¶
Overall: Hyperparameter tuning has produced a highly stable and well-generalized Gradient Boosting Classifier, with an exceptionally tight training-to-validation F1 gap of just 0.0007 — comparable to the tuned AdaBoost Classifier's gap of 0.0004. While AdaBoost retains a marginal edge in generalization consistency, the Gradient Boosting Classifier records the highest recall scores among all tuned models, making it particularly well-suited for use cases where minimizing missed Certified cases is a priority. Together, both models represent the strongest candidates for final model selection, with the choice between them likely depending on the specific performance criteria prioritized in deployment.¶

Based on the tuned XGBoost Classifier's performance on both the training and validation sets, the following observations can be made:¶

F1 Score: The tuned XGBoost Classifier achieves an F1 score of 0.8464 on the training set and 0.8218 on the validation set, with a difference of 0.0246 between the two. While this gap is considerably smaller than that of the untuned model, it remains the largest overfitting margin among the three boosting-based models evaluated — indicating that hyperparameter tuning has improved but not fully resolved the model's tendency to overfit.¶
Recall: The model records exceptionally high recall scores of 0.9795 on the training set and 0.9468 on the validation set — the highest recall figures observed across all tuned models in this analysis. This confirms that the XGBoost Classifier is highly effective at capturing the vast majority of actual Certified visa applications, with very few true positives being missed on either set.¶
Precision: Precision scores of 0.7451 on the training set and 0.7259 on the validation set, while still acceptable, are the lowest among the three tuned boosting models. The notable gap between XGBoost's recall and precision scores suggests that the model's aggressive identification of Certified cases comes at the cost of a higher rate of false positives — meaning it is more likely than AdaBoost or Gradient Boosting to incorrectly predict a Denied application as Certified.¶
Overall: The tuned XGBoost Classifier demonstrates strong predictive power, particularly in its ability to identify Certified cases, as evidenced by its industry-leading recall scores. However, its comparatively lower precision and larger training-to-validation F1 gap position it slightly behind the tuned AdaBoost and Gradient Boosting models in terms of overall balance and generalization stability.¶

Model Comparison and Final Model Selection¶

Comparing all models¶

def model_performance_classification_sklearn(model, predictors, target):
    """
    Function to compute different metrics to check classification model performance
    """
    # Predicting using the independent variables
    pred = model.predict(predictors)

    acc = metrics.accuracy_score(target, pred)  # to compute Accuracy
    recall = metrics.recall_score(target, pred)  # to compute Recall
    precision = metrics.precision_score(target, pred)  # to compute Precision
    f1 = metrics.f1_score(target, pred)  # to compute F1-score

    # Creating a dataframe of metrics
    df_perf = pd.DataFrame(
        {
            "Accuracy": acc,
            "Recall": recall,
            "Precision": precision,
            "F1": f1,
        },
        index=[0],
    )

    return df_perf

Based on the tuned XGBoost Classifier's performance on the unseen test set, the following observations can be made:¶

Accuracy: The model achieves an overall accuracy of approximately 71.31% on the test set, representing the proportion of total predictions — across both Certified and Denied cases — that were correctly classified.¶
Precision: The precision score of approximately 71.55% indicates that when the model predicts a visa application as Certified, it is correct roughly 71.55% of the time. Consequently, approximately 28.45% of applications predicted as Certified were actually Denied in the ground truth, reflecting a moderate rate of false positives. This suggests that the model leans toward approving applications rather than risking the misclassification of a genuinely qualified candidate.¶
Recall: The model records an exceptionally high recall score of approximately 94.71%, confirming that it correctly identifies nearly 95% of all truly Certified applications. This is the model's most notable strength — very few deserving applications are incorrectly flagged for denial, making the model highly reliable for minimizing missed certifications.¶
F1-Score: The F1-score of approximately 81.52% reflects a strong balance between precision and recall, and is notably higher than the overall accuracy of 71.31%. This divergence indicates that the model performs particularly well on the majority class (Certified) and that accuracy alone would underrepresent the model's true predictive capability in the presence of class imbalance.¶
Overall Inference: The tuned XGBoost Classifier demonstrates strong predictive performance on the test set, particularly in its ability to correctly identify the vast majority of Certified visa applications — a quality that makes it well-suited for deployment in scenarios where minimizing missed certifications is the primary objective. However, the gap between recall (94.71%) and precision (71.55%) highlights a precision-recall trade-off that warrants consideration. The relatively higher false positive rate means the model will occasionally certify applications that should have been denied, which may have operational implications depending on the cost associated with such errors. Should reducing false positives become a priority, further refinement through threshold adjustment, additional feature engineering, or alternative model configurations may be worth exploring.¶

Based on the feature importance plot, the following observations can be made regarding the factors that most significantly influence visa certification predictions:¶

prevailing_wage — Most Influential Feature: Prevailing wage emerges as the single most important feature in the model, exerting the greatest influence on predictions. This reinforces the earlier analytical observation that while wage distributions overlap between Certified and Denied cases, the specific wage amount nonetheless plays a decisive role in the model's decision-making. Higher wages likely signal more specialized roles, which are more readily certified by the Office of Foreign Labor Certification (OFLC).¶
continent_Asia and education_of_employee_Master's — High Importance: The applicant's continent of origin — particularly Asia, which accounts for the largest share of applications in the dataset — and the attainment of a Master's degree rank among the most influential predictors. This is consistent with the earlier bivariate analysis, which identified both continental origin and education level as strong differentiators between Certified and Denied outcomes.¶
has_job_experience_Y and unit_of_wage_Year — Moderate Importance: Prior job experience and an annual wage structure contribute meaningfully to the model's predictions, reflecting the OFLC's prioritization of candidates who can immediately address skill shortages and whose compensation arrangements align with the expectations of full-time, salaried employment.¶
Supporting Features — Lower but Notable Importance: Features such as yr_of_estab, no_of_employees, region_of_employment, and other education level indicators contribute to the model's predictions to a lesser extent. Notably, yr_of_estab may serve as a proxy for employer stability and compliance history, while regional features reflect the varying economic demand for visa-sponsored roles across different parts of the country.¶
Overall Inference: The model's predictions are primarily driven by a combination of financial factors (prevailing_wage, unit_of_wage_Year), applicant qualifications (education_of_employee_Master's, has_job_experience_Y), and demographic characteristics (continent_Asia). This suggests that visa certification outcomes in this dataset are most strongly influenced by the specialization and earning potential of the role, as well as the qualifications and background of the applicant — findings that are consistent with the broader objectives of employment-based visa programs, which aim to fill roles that cannot readily be occupied by the existing domestic workforce.¶
In [ ]:

Based on the data analysis, the performance of the Tuned XGBoost model, and the feature importance rankings, here are the , conclusions, actionable insights, and recommendations for EasyVisa and the Office of Foreign Labor Certification (OFLC).¶

Conclusions¶

Data Quality: The dataset was relatively clean, with no missing values or duplicate records. However, an anomaly in no_of_employees — specifically the presence of negative values — was identified and corrected during preprocessing. Additionally, the extremely low minimum values observed in prevailing_wage warrant further investigation, as they may represent data entry errors that could affect model reliability.¶
Class Imbalance: The target variable (case_status) is imbalanced, with Certified cases significantly outnumbering Denied cases. This imbalance was addressed during model training through oversampling techniques, with SMOTE ultimately proving more effective than undersampling in preserving model performance.¶
Key Determinants of Certification: Education level, prior job experience, continent of origin — particularly Asia — and the unit of wage (annual vs. hourly) emerged as strong predictors of visa certification, consistent with the patterns identified during exploratory data analysis.¶
Prevailing Wage Impact: While prevailing_wage is the single most important feature according to the model, its distribution largely overlaps between Certified and Denied cases. This suggests a complex, non-linear relationship rather than a simple wage threshold, implying that wage amount interacts with other features — such as region and education level — to influence certification outcomes.¶
Company Attributes: The number of employees and year of establishment do not exhibit a strong individual correlation with visa status, indicating that company size and age alone are not decisive factors in determining certification outcomes. These features contribute modestly to the model when considered alongside stronger predictors.¶
Model Performance: Ensemble boosting models — particularly AdaBoost, Gradient Boosting, and XGBoost — demonstrated the most robust performance across all evaluation stages. Following hyperparameter tuning, the XGBoost Classifier achieved the strongest overall performance on the test set, recording a high recall of 94.71% at the expense of a moderately lower precision of 71.55%. This trade-off means the model excels at identifying Certified cases but will occasionally predict Certified for applications that should have been Denied.¶

Actionable Insights¶

Prioritize Education and Experience: Applicants holding Master's or Doctorate degrees and possessing prior job experience have a substantially higher likelihood of visa certification. This reflects a clear preference within the certification process for highly skilled and experienced professionals who can demonstrably fill roles that cannot be readily occupied by the existing domestic workforce.¶
Wage Unit as a Certification Signal: Positions offering an annual wage structure are significantly more likely to be certified than those offering hourly compensation. This likely reflects perceptions of greater job stability and adherence to the salary requirements associated with employment-based visa categories.¶
Continental Trends Inform Recruitment Strategy: While Asia contributes the highest volume of applications, Europe records a notably higher certification rate. This divergence may inform targeted recruitment strategies or prompt policy reviews regarding the types of roles and qualifications most commonly associated with applicants from each region.¶
Prevailing Wage Compliance is Critical: Given that prevailing_wage is the most influential feature in the model, ensuring that applications meet or exceed the prevailing wage standard for the relevant role and region is essential for maximizing certification success — even where the direct relationship between wage and outcome is non-linear.¶
Manage the Precision-Recall Trade-off: The XGBoost model's higher recall relative to precision means it will rarely miss a genuinely Certified case, but will occasionally predict Certified for applications that should be Denied. Where the operational cost of false positives is high, further model refinement — such as threshold adjustment or the adoption of cost-sensitive learning — should be considered.¶

Recommendations¶

Data Validation for Prevailing Wage: Investigate the extremely low prevailing_wage values identified during preprocessing and implement data validation rules at the point of entry to prevent such anomalies from propagating into future model training cycles, as they could compromise prediction reliability.¶
Strategic Application Guidance: Advise applicants to clearly highlight higher educational qualifications and relevant job experience in their applications. For sponsoring employers, offering annual wage structures where feasible — rather than hourly arrangements — is recommended to improve certification prospects.¶

Implement a Tiered Review System (OFLC): A risk-based, tiered approach to application review could significantly improve processing efficiency:¶

Tier 1 — Expedited Approval: Applications meeting strong certification criteria (Master's degree or higher, high prevailing wage, established employer, prior experience) may be candidates for streamlined or automated certification, potentially reducing manual review workload considerably.¶
Tier 2 — Priority Review: Applications where the model predicts Certified but with a borderline confidence score (e.g., between 0.50 and 0.70) should be flagged for closer human review.¶
Tier 3 — Mandatory Audit: All applications predicted as Denied, as well as those involving recently established companies or applicants with only a High School education, should be subject to mandatory manual audit.¶
Threshold Tuning for Precision Improvement: Rather than relying on the default classification threshold of 0.50, adjusting the threshold upward (e.g., to 0.65–0.70) would increase precision — ensuring that when the model predicts Certified, it does so with greater confidence — at the cost of a modest reduction in recall. This adjustment may be appropriate in contexts where the cost of false positives is elevated.¶
Address Class Imbalance with Cost-Sensitive Learning: Given the model's current tendency toward false positives, implementing cost-sensitive learning — which penalizes the model more heavily for incorrectly predicting Denied cases as Certified — could improve the balance between precision and recall without sacrificing the volume of training data.¶
Incorporate Occupation-Specific Data: The current model relies on broad regional and categorical features. Incorporating Standard Occupational Classification (SOC) codes into future iterations would provide a more granular basis for wage competitiveness assessments and could meaningfully improve the model's ability to evaluate whether a given wage is truly aligned with the role and region in question.¶
Continuous Monitoring and Retraining: Model performance should be monitored regularly on incoming data, and the model should be retrained periodically to account for evolving visa policies, labor market dynamics, and shifts in feature importance over time.¶
Explore Explainable AI (XAI) Techniques: Given the high-stakes nature of visa certification decisions, the adoption of explainability tools such as SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) values is strongly recommended. These techniques would enable granular, case-level explanations for individual predictions — going beyond aggregate feature importance to clarify why a specific application was predicted as Certified or Denied — thereby improving transparency and supporting human oversight of model decisions.¶
